{{Short description|Water deity}}
[[File:Zenkenkojitsu-vol01-no18-Agatamori.jpg|thumb|350px|Agatamori battling mizuchi in the pool. From ''Zenken kojitsu'' (1878)]]
The {{nihongo|'''''Mizuchi'''''|大虬, 蛟龍, 蛟, 美都知|}} is a type of {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|WD=Q2366503|lt=Japanese dragon|1=Japanese dragon}} or legendary serpent-like creature, either found in an aquatic habitat or otherwise connected to water. Some commentators perceived it to have been a [[:en:Water deity|Water deity]]. It is described in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and one ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'' poem.

== Etymology ==
In olden times pronounced ''mi-tsu-chi'', the word can be broken down to ''mi'' "water" + ''tsu'' a {{ill|Japanese particles|en|Japanese particles|WD=Q1480213|lt=particle|1=Japanese particles}} meaning "of" + ''chi'' "spirit".{{r|KojienMizuchi1991}} The ''-chi'' is glossed as a word root used only as a part of a compound word{{r|KojienChi1991}} (as a {{ill|Suffix|en|Suffix|WD=Q102047|lt=Suffix|1=Suffix}}, etc.)

== Chinese character representation ==
''Mizuchi'' is also the [[:en:Kun-yomi|Japanese transliteration]] for several Chinese [[:en:glyphs|glyphs]],{{r|KojienMizuchi1976}} each glyph putatively representing a type of {{ill|Chinese dragon|en|Chinese dragon|WD=Q215605|lt=Chinese dragon|1=Chinese dragon}}: namely the  ''{{ill|Jiaolong|en|Jiaolong|WD=Q16241852|lt=jiāolóng|1=Jiaolong}}'' ([[Wikt:蛟|蛟竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kōryū}}) or "4-legged dragon", the ''{{ill|qiulong|en|qiulong|WD=Q7267959|lt=qiúlóng|1=Qiulong}}'' ([[Wikt:虬|虬竜]] or [[Wikt:虯|虯竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kyūryū}}) or "hornless dragon" and the ''[[chilong|chīlóng]]'' ([[Wikt:螭|螭竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|chiryū}}) or "yellow dragon".

F. J. Daniels{{Efn|Emeritus Professor of Japanese at University of London, died August 1983.{{r|blacker1983}}}} cautions that for {{nihongo|''[[kuraokami|okami]]''|龗}} and ''mizuchi'', "it is unsafe to deduce their forms from the Chinese characters allotted to them".{{r|Daniels1960_157}} [[Kunio Yanagita]] also emphasized that while the use of character like 虬 may suggest a snake-like being, it should be stressed that the ''mizuchi'' signifies a "water spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}

==Early references==
The ancient chronicle ''[[Nihon Shoki|Nihongi]]'' contains references to ''mizuchi''. Under the 67th year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Emperor Nintoku|1=Emperor Nintoku}} (conventionally dated 379 AD), it is mentioned that in central {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Province|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, at a fork on Kawashima River (川嶋河, old name of {{ill|Takahashi River|en|Takahashi River|WD=Q1132339|lt=Takahashi River|1=Takahashi River}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}), a great water serpent or dragon (大虬) dwelt and would breathe or spew out its venom, poisoning and killing many passersby.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The text designates the creature as a qiulong (虬/虯) in Chinese prose (''{{ill|Kanbun|en|Kanbun|WD=Q7901319|lt=Kanbun|1=Kanbun}}''), but the annotation gives its Japanese reading as ''mitsuchi''.{{r|ishizuka2007_38}}}}{{r|nihonshoki_jtext}}

This ''mizuchi'' was exterminated by a man named {{Nihongo|Agatamori|県守|}}, ancestor of the {{Nihongo|Kasa-no-omi|笠臣|}} clan. He approached the pool of the river, cast three {{ill|Calabash|en|Calabash|WD=Q1277255|lt=Calabash|1=Calabash}}es which floated to the surface of the water and challenged the beast to make these gourds sink, threatening to slay it should it fail. The beast transformed into a deer and tried unsuccessfully to sink them, whereby the man slew the monster. The record goes on to say: "...He further sought out the water-dragon's fellows. Now the tribe of all the water-dragons filled a cave in the bottom of the pool. He slew them every one and the water of the river became changed to blood. Therefore that water was called the pool of Agatamori".{{r|Nihon67}}<ref>Tr. {{harvp|Aston|1896|loc='''1''', p. 299}}.</ref>

A river-god reported seen in Nintoku 11 (putatively 323 AD) is also regarded by commentators to be a mizuchi, due to paralleling circumstances. On that year, the {{illm|Mamuta dikes|ja|茨田堤}} built along {{ill|Yodo River|en|Yodo River|WD=Q1140505|lt=Yodo River|1=Yodo River}} kept getting breached and the Emperor guided by an oracular dream ordered two men, Kowa-kubi from {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province|1=Musashi Province}} and Koromo-no-ko from {{ill|Kawachi Province|en|Kawachi Province|WD=Q1047150|lt=Kawachi Province|1=Kawachi Province}} be sought ought and sacrificed to the "'''River God'''" or {{Nihongo|[[:en:Kawa-no-kami|Kawa-no-kami]]|河伯|}}.{{Efn|Note that 河伯 in China designates the ''{{ill|Hebo|en|Hebo|WD=Q10521939|lt=Hebo|1=Hebo}}'' deity.}} One of the men, who resisted being sacrificed, employed the floating calabash and dared the River God to sink it as proof to show it was truly divine will that demanded him as sacrifice. A whirlwind came and tried, but the calabash just floated away, and thus he extricated himself from death using his wits. Although River God is not called ''mizuchi'' in the source, [[William George Aston|Aston]] has regarded the River God (Kawa-no-kami) and the ''mizuchi'' as equivalent.{{r|Aston1905_1_1501}}

{{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser{{!}}Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}} concludes, "From this passage, we learn that in ancient times human sacrifices were made to the dragon-shaped river-gods".{{r|Visser1913_139}} {{ill|Michael Foster (folklorist)|en|Michael Foster (folklorist)|WD=Q6830379|lt=Michael Dylan Foster|1=Michael Foster (folklorist)}}
suggests this is "perhaps the first documented appearance of the water spirit that would become known popularly in Japan as the {{ill|Kappa (folklore)|en|Kappa (folklore)|WD=Q335140|lt=kappa|1=Kappa (folklore)}}".{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=2}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In [[Japanese folklore]] the ''kappa'' is a [[:en:water sprite|water sprite]] often considered benignly mischievous,{{sfnp|Foster|1998|pp=1, 4}} (and thus may appear unlike a sacrifice-demanding serpent).  But the ''kappa'' can also be seen as sinister, reaching in and extracting the liver or the ''shirikodama'' from humans.{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=6}}}}

A mizuchi is also mentioned in the {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}, the ancient collection of Japanese poems. The {{ill|Waka (poetry)|en|Waka (poetry)|WD=Q737148|lt=tanka|1=Waka (poetry)}} poem #3833 composed by {{illm|Prince Sakaibe|ja|境部王}}<ref name=sakaibe-origtext>[[#manyoshu3833|''Man'yōshū'' #3833]] by Prince Saikabe, original text:"虎尓乗 古屋乎越而 青淵尓 鮫龍取将来 劒刀毛我"</ref> can be loosely paraphrased to mean "I could ride a tiger to leap over the Old Shack, to the green pool, to take down the ''mizuchi'' dragon there, if only I had a sword capable of doing just that".{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The shark (鮫) character in the poem's original text is emended to the mizuchi (蛟) character. {{illm|Kariya Ekisai|ja|狩谷棭斎}} in his annotation to the ''[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]'' remarks: "Considering the ''Manyōshū'' (quote follows).. the ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` shark-dragon´ is actually ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` flood dragon´, and correctly read as ` ''midzuchi''´ 万葉集を按ずに.. 鮫龍即蛟龍也、宜しく美都知と訓ず".{{r|kariya1883}}}}{{r|Takeda1972_1PLUS|Ito2005_475PLUS}}

== Folklorist studies ==
Polymath {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}}, in his essay {{Nihongo|''Jūnishi kō: mi(hebi)''|『十二支考』|"A Study of Twelve Animals of Chinese Zodiac"}} states "Even in our country (Japan), the various snakes that dwelled by water and were feared by people seemed to have been called ''mizuchi,'' or 'master of the water'".{{r|Minakata1917}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}} Here Minakata draws on [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] scholar {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|WD=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}}' suggestion that the ''-chi'' signified an {{ill|Honorific|en|Honorific|WD=Q1326966|lt=Honorific|1=Honorific}}.{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Minakata misquoted Norinaga, but Norinaga said ''chi'' was the honorific. Minakata wrote: "When Motoori Norinaga said ''tsuchi'' was an honorific, he must have interpreted it as a master of water or somesuch 本居宣長はツチは尊称だと言ったは、水の主ぬしくらいに解いたのだろ".{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}} What Norinaga actually stated was "there are many examples of [deities' names that are called]  so-and-so ''-zuchi'', where ''zu'' is a word akin to "of" while ''chi'' is an honorific 某豆知（なにづち）と云例あまたありて..豆（づ）は之（の）に通ふ辞、知（ち）は称名（たたへな）なり".{{r|Motoori1822}}}} As stated above folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita|Yanagita]] emphasized the meaning of ''chi'' as "spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}

=== Corruption into kappa ===
Minakata also conjectured that in some parts of the country, ''mizuchi'' eventually came to be regarded as creatures of the ''kappa'' kind. This is because the ''kappa'' creatures are known locally by many names that sound much like ''mizuchi'', such as ''mizushi'' (former {{ill|Noto Province|en|Noto Province|WD=Q1047671|lt=Noto Province|1=Noto Province}}, {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|en|Ishikawa Prefecture|WD=Q131281|lt=Ishikawa Prefecture|1=Ishikawa Prefecture}}), ''medochi'' ([[:en:Nanbu Domain|Nanbu]] region, parts of {{ill|Iwate Prefecture|en|Iwate Prefecture|WD=Q48326|lt=Iwate|1=Iwate Prefecture}}, {{ill|Aomori Prefecture|en|Aomori Prefecture|WD=Q71699|lt=Aomori|1=Aomori Prefecture}}, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|en|Akita Prefecture|WD=Q81863|lt=Akita|1=Akita Prefecture}}), ''mintsuchi'' ({{ill|Ezo|en|Ezo|WD=Q1040184|lt=Ezo|1=Ezo}}, now [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]).{{sfnmp|Minakata|1984|1p=117|Minakata|1984b|2p=159}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Cf. other local synonyms of ''kappa'' such as ''medochi'' ([[:en:Ehime prefecture|Ehime prefecture]]) and ''mizushi'' ([[:en:Fukui prefecture|Fukui prefecture]]) mentioned by Asakawa Zen'an's ''Zen'an zuihitsu''.{{r|Asakawa1927_33940}}}}

Furthermore, in the lore of {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} ({{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture|1=Niigata Prefecture}}), the kappa was said to abhor the calabash gourd,<ref>Yanagita, Kunio (1914), ''Santō mintan shū'', p. 84, cited by Minakata</ref> which is reminiscent of the episodes in ''Nihon Shoki'' where the River God or ''mizuchi'' are challenged to submerge the calabashes.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=117}} Similar observations are made by folklorists Yanagita{{r|Yanagita2014_133}} and Jun'ichirō Ishikawa.{{r|Ishikawa1985_4550645248}}

Minakata was also encouraged by the fact that the snake and the kappa (alongside the [[:en:suppon|suppon]] soft-shelled turtle) were grouped as three creatures known to kill humans in water by {{illm|Asakawa Zen'an|ja|朝川善庵}}'s essay ''Zen'an zuihitsu'' and conjectured that there used to be lore where sacred snakes which were "masters of the body of water" would transform into human form and wreak havoc, but terms such as ''mizushi'' became reserved for the kappa-kind, whereas the terms to refer to the "masters of the body of water" as ''mizuchi'' became forgotten.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Mizuchi]][[fa:میزوچی]][[fr:Mizuchi]][[hu:Mizucsi]][[it:Mizuchi]][[ja:蛟]]

{{Short description|Water deity}}
[[File:Zenkenkojitsu-vol01-no18-Agatamori.jpg|thumb|350px|Agatamori battling mizuchi in the pool. From ''Zenken kojitsu'' (1878)]]
The {{nihongo|'''''Mizuchi'''''|大虬, 蛟龍, 蛟, 美都知|}} is a type of {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|WD=Q2366503|lt=Japanese dragon|1=Japanese dragon}} or legendary serpent-like creature, either found in an aquatic habitat or otherwise connected to water. Some commentators perceived it to have been a [[:en:Water deity|Water deity]]. It is described in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and one ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'' poem.

== Etymology ==
In olden times pronounced ''mi-tsu-chi'', the word can be broken down to ''mi'' "water" + ''tsu'' a {{ill|Japanese particles|en|Japanese particles|WD=Q1480213|lt=particle|1=Japanese particles}} meaning "of" + ''chi'' "spirit".{{r|KojienMizuchi1991}} The ''-chi'' is glossed as a word root used only as a part of a compound word{{r|KojienChi1991}} (as a {{ill|Suffix|en|Suffix|WD=Q102047|lt=Suffix|1=Suffix}}, etc.)

== Chinese character representation ==
''Mizuchi'' is also the [[:en:Kun-yomi|Japanese transliteration]] for several Chinese [[:en:glyphs|glyphs]],{{r|KojienMizuchi1976}} each glyph putatively representing a type of {{ill|Chinese dragon|en|Chinese dragon|WD=Q215605|lt=Chinese dragon|1=Chinese dragon}}: namely the  ''{{ill|Jiaolong|en|Jiaolong|WD=Q16241852|lt=jiāolóng|1=Jiaolong}}'' ([[Wikt:蛟|蛟竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kōryū}}) or "4-legged dragon", the ''{{ill|qiulong|en|qiulong|WD=Q7267959|lt=qiúlóng|1=Qiulong}}'' ([[Wikt:虬|虬竜]] or [[Wikt:虯|虯竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kyūryū}}) or "hornless dragon" and the ''[[chilong|chīlóng]]'' ([[Wikt:螭|螭竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|chiryū}}) or "yellow dragon".

F. J. Daniels{{Efn|Emeritus Professor of Japanese at University of London, died August 1983.{{r|blacker1983}}}} cautions that for {{nihongo|''[[kuraokami|okami]]''|龗}} and ''mizuchi'', "it is unsafe to deduce their forms from the Chinese characters allotted to them".{{r|Daniels1960_157}} [[Kunio Yanagita]] also emphasized that while the use of character like 虬 may suggest a snake-like being, it should be stressed that the ''mizuchi'' signifies a "water spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}

==Early references==
The ancient chronicle ''[[Nihon Shoki|Nihongi]]'' contains references to ''mizuchi''. Under the 67th year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Emperor Nintoku|1=Emperor Nintoku}} (conventionally dated 379 AD), it is mentioned that in central {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Province|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, at a fork on Kawashima River (川嶋河, old name of {{ill|Takahashi River|en|Takahashi River|WD=Q1132339|lt=Takahashi River|1=Takahashi River}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}), a great water serpent or dragon (大虬) dwelt and would breathe or spew out its venom, poisoning and killing many passersby.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The text designates the creature as a qiulong (虬/虯) in Chinese prose (''{{ill|Kanbun|en|Kanbun|WD=Q7901319|lt=Kanbun|1=Kanbun}}''), but the annotation gives its Japanese reading as ''mitsuchi''.{{r|ishizuka2007_38}}}}{{r|nihonshoki_jtext}}

This ''mizuchi'' was exterminated by a man named {{Nihongo|Agatamori|県守|}}, ancestor of the {{Nihongo|Kasa-no-omi|笠臣|}} clan. He approached the pool of the river, cast three {{ill|Calabash|en|Calabash|WD=Q1277255|lt=Calabash|1=Calabash}}es which floated to the surface of the water and challenged the beast to make these gourds sink, threatening to slay it should it fail. The beast transformed into a deer and tried unsuccessfully to sink them, whereby the man slew the monster. The record goes on to say: "...He further sought out the water-dragon's fellows. Now the tribe of all the water-dragons filled a cave in the bottom of the pool. He slew them every one and the water of the river became changed to blood. Therefore that water was called the pool of Agatamori".{{r|Nihon67}}<ref>Tr. {{harvp|Aston|1896|loc='''1''', p. 299}}.</ref>

A river-god reported seen in Nintoku 11 (putatively 323 AD) is also regarded by commentators to be a mizuchi, due to paralleling circumstances. On that year, the {{illm|Mamuta dikes|ja|茨田堤}} built along {{ill|Yodo River|en|Yodo River|WD=Q1140505|lt=Yodo River|1=Yodo River}} kept getting breached and the Emperor guided by an oracular dream ordered two men, Kowa-kubi from {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province|1=Musashi Province}} and Koromo-no-ko from {{ill|Kawachi Province|en|Kawachi Province|WD=Q1047150|lt=Kawachi Province|1=Kawachi Province}} be sought ought and sacrificed to the "'''River God'''" or {{Nihongo|[[:en:Kawa-no-kami|Kawa-no-kami]]|河伯|}}.{{Efn|Note that 河伯 in China designates the ''{{ill|Hebo|en|Hebo|WD=Q10521939|lt=Hebo|1=Hebo}}'' deity.}} One of the men, who resisted being sacrificed, employed the floating calabash and dared the River God to sink it as proof to show it was truly divine will that demanded him as sacrifice. A whirlwind came and tried, but the calabash just floated away, and thus he extricated himself from death using his wits. Although River God is not called ''mizuchi'' in the source, [[William George Aston|Aston]] has regarded the River God (Kawa-no-kami) and the ''mizuchi'' as equivalent.{{r|Aston1905_1_1501}}

{{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser{{!}}Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}} concludes, "From this passage, we learn that in ancient times human sacrifices were made to the dragon-shaped river-gods".{{r|Visser1913_139}} {{ill|Michael Foster (folklorist)|en|Michael Foster (folklorist)|WD=Q6830379|lt=Michael Dylan Foster|1=Michael Foster (folklorist)}}
suggests this is "perhaps the first documented appearance of the water spirit that would become known popularly in Japan as the {{ill|Kappa (folklore)|en|Kappa (folklore)|WD=Q335140|lt=kappa|1=Kappa (folklore)}}".{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=2}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In [[Japanese folklore]] the ''kappa'' is a [[:en:water sprite|water sprite]] often considered benignly mischievous,{{sfnp|Foster|1998|pp=1, 4}} (and thus may appear unlike a sacrifice-demanding serpent).  But the ''kappa'' can also be seen as sinister, reaching in and extracting the liver or the ''shirikodama'' from humans.{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=6}}}}

A mizuchi is also mentioned in the {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}, the ancient collection of Japanese poems. The {{ill|Waka (poetry)|en|Waka (poetry)|WD=Q737148|lt=tanka|1=Waka (poetry)}} poem #3833 composed by {{illm|Prince Sakaibe|ja|境部王}}<ref name=sakaibe-origtext>[[#manyoshu3833|''Man'yōshū'' #3833]] by Prince Saikabe, original text:"虎尓乗 古屋乎越而 青淵尓 鮫龍取将来 劒刀毛我"</ref> can be loosely paraphrased to mean "I could ride a tiger to leap over the Old Shack, to the green pool, to take down the ''mizuchi'' dragon there, if only I had a sword capable of doing just that".{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The shark (鮫) character in the poem's original text is emended to the mizuchi (蛟) character. {{illm|Kariya Ekisai|ja|狩谷棭斎}} in his annotation to the ''[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]'' remarks: "Considering the ''Manyōshū'' (quote follows).. the ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` shark-dragon´ is actually ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` flood dragon´, and correctly read as ` ''midzuchi''´ 万葉集を按ずに.. 鮫龍即蛟龍也、宜しく美都知と訓ず".{{r|kariya1883}}}}{{r|Takeda1972_1PLUS|Ito2005_475PLUS}}

== Folklorist studies ==
Polymath {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}}, in his essay {{Nihongo|''Jūnishi kō: mi(hebi)''|『十二支考』|"A Study of Twelve Animals of Chinese Zodiac"}} states "Even in our country (Japan), the various snakes that dwelled by water and were feared by people seemed to have been called ''mizuchi,'' or 'master of the water'".{{r|Minakata1917}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}} Here Minakata draws on [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] scholar {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|WD=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}}' suggestion that the ''-chi'' signified an {{ill|Honorific|en|Honorific|WD=Q1326966|lt=Honorific|1=Honorific}}.{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Minakata misquoted Norinaga, but Norinaga said ''chi'' was the honorific. Minakata wrote: "When Motoori Norinaga said ''tsuchi'' was an honorific, he must have interpreted it as a master of water or somesuch 本居宣長はツチは尊称だと言ったは、水の主ぬしくらいに解いたのだろ".{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}} What Norinaga actually stated was "there are many examples of [deities' names that are called]  so-and-so ''-zuchi'', where ''zu'' is a word akin to "of" while ''chi'' is an honorific 某豆知（なにづち）と云例あまたありて..豆（づ）は之（の）に通ふ辞、知（ち）は称名（たたへな）なり".{{r|Motoori1822}}}} As stated above folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita|Yanagita]] emphasized the meaning of ''chi'' as "spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}

=== Corruption into kappa ===
Minakata also conjectured that in some parts of the country, ''mizuchi'' eventually came to be regarded as creatures of the ''kappa'' kind. This is because the ''kappa'' creatures are known locally by many names that sound much like ''mizuchi'', such as ''mizushi'' (former {{ill|Noto Province|en|Noto Province|WD=Q1047671|lt=Noto Province|1=Noto Province}}, {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|en|Ishikawa Prefecture|WD=Q131281|lt=Ishikawa Prefecture|1=Ishikawa Prefecture}}), ''medochi'' ([[:en:Nanbu Domain|Nanbu]] region, parts of {{ill|Iwate Prefecture|en|Iwate Prefecture|WD=Q48326|lt=Iwate|1=Iwate Prefecture}}, {{ill|Aomori Prefecture|en|Aomori Prefecture|WD=Q71699|lt=Aomori|1=Aomori Prefecture}}, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|en|Akita Prefecture|WD=Q81863|lt=Akita|1=Akita Prefecture}}), ''mintsuchi'' ({{ill|Ezo|en|Ezo|WD=Q1040184|lt=Ezo|1=Ezo}}, now [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]).{{sfnmp|Minakata|1984|1p=117|Minakata|1984b|2p=159}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Cf. other local synonyms of ''kappa'' such as ''medochi'' ([[:en:Ehime prefecture|Ehime prefecture]]) and ''mizushi'' ([[:en:Fukui prefecture|Fukui prefecture]]) mentioned by Asakawa Zen'an's ''Zen'an zuihitsu''.{{r|Asakawa1927_33940}}}}

Furthermore, in the lore of {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} ({{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture|1=Niigata Prefecture}}), the kappa was said to abhor the calabash gourd,<ref>Yanagita, Kunio (1914), ''Santō mintan shū'', p. 84, cited by Minakata</ref> which is reminiscent of the episodes in ''Nihon Shoki'' where the River God or ''mizuchi'' are challenged to submerge the calabashes.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=117}} Similar observations are made by folklorists Yanagita{{r|Yanagita2014_133}} and Jun'ichirō Ishikawa.{{r|Ishikawa1985_4550645248}}

Minakata was also encouraged by the fact that the snake and the kappa (alongside the [[:en:suppon|suppon]] soft-shelled turtle) were grouped as three creatures known to kill humans in water by {{illm|Asakawa Zen'an|ja|朝川善庵}}'s essay ''Zen'an zuihitsu'' and conjectured that there used to be lore where sacred snakes which were "masters of the body of water" would transform into human form and wreak havoc, but terms such as ''mizushi'' became reserved for the kappa-kind, whereas the terms to refer to the "masters of the body of water" as ''mizuchi'' became forgotten.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}}

==In popular culture==
;(vehicles, vessels)
* ''{{illm|Kōryū (submarine)|ja|蛟竜 (潜水艦)}}'' ({{langx|ja|蛟竜}}), (synonymous with ''mizuchi''),  an ex-Japanese Navy submarine.
* ''{{ill|Jiaolong (submersible)|en|Jiaolong (submersible)|WD=Q1546594|lt=Jiaolong|1=Jiaolong (submersible)}}'' ({{zh|蛟龙号}}), a Chinese deep-ocean {{ill|submersible|en|submersible|WD=Q1570255|lt=submersible|1=Submersible}}.
;(novels)
* {{Nihongo|"''Mizuchi''"|『[[:ja:水霊 ミズチ|水霊 ミズチ]]』}}, a 1998 horror novel by {{illm|Hirohumi Tanaka|ja|田中啓文}} and its 2006 horror movie adaptation directed by {{illm|Kiyoshi Yamamoto|ja|山本清史}}, entitled "Death Water" in English, though theme is "water spirit" and not dragon.
* ''{{ill|Sohryuden: Legend of the Dragon Kings|en|Sohryuden: Legend of the Dragon Kings|WD=Q836021|lt=Sohryuden: Legend of the Dragon Kings|1=Sohryuden: Legend of the Dragon Kings}}'' (novel) – A man named {{Nihongo|Mizuchi|水池}} is an allusion.
* In Andrew Rowe's ''Arcane Ascension'' series, Mizuchi, also known as Hero's End or Guardian of Secrets, is a giant water serpent, spire guardian of the Serpent Spire, and one of the God Serpent's daughters.

;(manga, anime)
* ''{{ill|Eight Clouds Rising|en|Eight Clouds Rising|WD=Q5348960|lt=Eight Clouds Rising|1=Eight Clouds Rising}}'' – {{Nihongo|Mizuchi|水蛇|"Watersnake"}} is one of seven divine swords.
* ''[[:en:GeGeGe no Kitaro|GeGeGe no Kitaro]]'' (manga, anime) – a ''kōryū'' (syn. ''mizuchi'') appears as adversary.
* ''{{ill|Omamori Himari|en|Omamori Himari|WD=Q1203079|lt=Omamori Himari|1=Omamori Himari}}'' (manga, novella, anime) – the character Shizuku is a mizuchi.
* ''[[:en:Our Home's Fox Deity.|Our Home's Fox Deity.]]'' – A [[miko]] priestess is possessed by a mizuchi.
* ''{{ill|Samurai Deeper Kyo|en|Samurai Deeper Kyo|WD=Q621603|lt=Samurai Deeper Kyo|1=Samurai Deeper Kyo}}'' (manga) – {{ill|Demon Eyes Kyo|en|Demon Eyes Kyo|WD=Q3200962|lt=Demon Eyes Kyo|1=Demon Eyes Kyo}} uses an attack called "''mizuchi''" in his sword fighting style. Compare Japanese ''kōryū'' or ''kōryō'' 蛟竜 "rain dragon; hidden genius; {{ill|Kaiten|en|Kaiten|WD=Q277621|lt=Kaiten|1=Kaiten}} torpedo".
* ''[[Noragami]]'' (manga, anime) – the character Nora is called Mizuchi by Father and is frequently shown walking over water.
* ''{{ill|Spirited Away|en|Spirited Away|WD=Q155653|lt=Spirited Away|1=Spirited Away}}'' (anime, movie) – the character Haku looks like a Mizuchi and he is a river spirit.
* ''{{ill|Inuyasha|en|Inuyasha|WD=Q182056|lt=Inuyasha|1=Inuyasha}}'' (manga) - the character a snake yokai called Mizuchi using its spit venom and poison mist.
* ''[[:en:Yashahime: Princess Half-Demon|Yashahime: Princess Half-Demon]]'' (anime) - the character a snake yokai called Mizuchi using its spit venom and poison mist.

;(games)
* ''{{illm|Mah-jong Fight Club|ja|麻雀格闘倶楽部}}'' (game) – player character becomes ''kōryū'' (one of the true dragons) when certain conditions are met.
* ''{{ill|Monster Hunter 2|en|Monster Hunter 2|WD=Q518560|lt=Monster Hunter 2|1=Monster Hunter 2}}'' (PS 2) – an elder dragon type named Ōnazuchi is a take on mizuchi; named Chameleos in English-language platforms.
* ''{{ill|Neo Geo Battle Coliseum|en|Neo Geo Battle Coliseum|WD=Q3275594|lt=Neo Geo Battle Coliseum|1=Neo Geo Battle Coliseum}}'' (game) – a boss character named Mizuchi, a clone of  {{ill|Orochi (The King of Fighters)|en|Orochi (The King of Fighters)|WD=Q10341589|lt=Orochi|1=Orochi (The King of Fighters)}} from ''{{ill|The King of Fighters|en|The King of Fighters|WD=Q340517|lt=The King of Fighters '97|1=The King of Fighters}}''
*''{{ill|Ōkamiden|en|Ōkamiden|WD=Q1054901|lt=Ōkamiden|1=Ōkamiden}}'' (game) – a water dragon boss that used to be the guardian of a seaside village.
*''{{ill|Nioh 2|en|Nioh 2|WD=Q67482292|lt=Nioh 2|1=Nioh 2}}'' (game) – there is a water dragon guardian spirit called Mizuchi that the player can be imbued to characters to gain protection and special effects.{{r|MizuchiNiohWeb}}
* ''{{ill|Sakuna: Of Rice and Ruin|en|Sakuna: Of Rice and Ruin|WD=Q97590136|lt=Sakuna: Of Rice and Ruin|1=Sakuna: Of Rice and Ruin}}'' (game) - The antagonist and final boss is a three headed water dragon named Omizuchi. The prefix o- is a Japanese honorific ([[:en:keigo|keigo]]).

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Mizuchi]][[fa:میزوچی]][[fr:Mizuchi]][[hu:Mizucsi]][[it:Mizuchi]][[ja:蛟]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Mizuchi]][[fa:میزوچی]][[fr:Mizuchi]][[hu:Mizucsi]][[it:Mizuchi]][[ja:蛟]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Mizuchi]][[fa:میزوچی]][[fr:Mizuchi]][[hu:Mizucsi]][[it:Mizuchi]][[ja:蛟]]
{{Short description|Water deity}} [[File:Zenkenkojitsu-vol01-no18-Agatamori.jpg|thumb|350px|Agatamori battling mizuchi in the pool. From ''Zenken kojitsu'' (1878)]] The {{nihongo|'''''Mizuchi'''''|大虬, 蛟龍, 蛟, 美都知|}} is a type of {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|qid=Q2366503|lt=Japanese dragon|1=Japanese dragon}} or legendary serpent-like creature, either found in an aquatic habitat or otherwise connected to water. Some commentators perceived it to have been a [[:en:Water deity|Water deity]]. It is described in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and one ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|qid=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'' poem.
== Etymology == In olden times pronounced ''mi-tsu-chi'', the word can be broken down to ''mi'' "water" + ''tsu'' a {{ill|Japanese particles|en|Japanese particles|qid=Q1480213|lt=particle|1=Japanese particles}} meaning "of" + ''chi'' "spirit".{{r|KojienMizuchi1991}} The ''-chi'' is glossed as a word root used only as a part of a compound word{{r|KojienChi1991}} (as a {{ill|Suffix|en|Suffix|qid=Q102047|lt=Suffix|1=Suffix}}, etc.)
== Chinese character representation == ''Mizuchi'' is also the [[:en:Kun-yomi|Japanese transliteration]] for several Chinese [[:en:glyphs|glyphs]],{{r|KojienMizuchi1976}} each glyph putatively representing a type of {{ill|Chinese dragon|en|Chinese dragon|qid=Q215605|lt=Chinese dragon|1=Chinese dragon}}: namely the ''{{ill|Jiaolong|en|Jiaolong|qid=Q16241852|lt=jiāolóng|1=Jiaolong}}'' ([[Wikt:蛟|蛟竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kōryū}}) or "4-legged dragon", the ''{{ill|qiulong|en|qiulong|qid=Q7267959|lt=qiúlóng|1=Qiulong}}'' ([[Wikt:虬|虬竜]] or [[Wikt:虯|虯竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|kyūryū}}) or "hornless dragon" and the ''[[chilong|chīlóng]]'' ([[Wikt:螭|螭竜]]; {{langx|ja-Latn|chiryū}}) or "yellow dragon".
F. J. Daniels{{Efn|Emeritus Professor of Japanese at University of London, died August 1983.{{r|blacker1983}}}} cautions that for {{nihongo|''[[kuraokami|okami]]''|龗}} and ''mizuchi'', "it is unsafe to deduce their forms from the Chinese characters allotted to them".{{r|Daniels1960_157}} [[Kunio Yanagita]] also emphasized that while the use of character like 虬 may suggest a snake-like being, it should be stressed that the ''mizuchi'' signifies a "water spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}
==Early references== The ancient chronicle ''[[Nihon Shoki|Nihongi]]'' contains references to ''mizuchi''. Under the 67th year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|qid=Q313119|lt=Emperor Nintoku|1=Emperor Nintoku}} (conventionally dated 379 AD), it is mentioned that in central {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|qid=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Province|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, at a fork on Kawashima River (川嶋河, old name of {{ill|Takahashi River|en|Takahashi River|qid=Q1132339|lt=Takahashi River|1=Takahashi River}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|qid=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}), a great water serpent or dragon (大虬) dwelt and would breathe or spew out its venom, poisoning and killing many passersby.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The text designates the creature as a qiulong (虬/虯) in Chinese prose (''{{ill|Kanbun|en|Kanbun|qid=Q7901319|lt=Kanbun|1=Kanbun}}''), but the annotation gives its Japanese reading as ''mitsuchi''.{{r|ishizuka2007_38}}}}{{r|nihonshoki_jtext}}
This ''mizuchi'' was exterminated by a man named {{Nihongo|Agatamori|県守|}}, ancestor of the {{Nihongo|Kasa-no-omi|笠臣|}} clan. He approached the pool of the river, cast three {{ill|Calabash|en|Calabash|qid=Q1277255|lt=Calabash|1=Calabash}}es which floated to the surface of the water and challenged the beast to make these gourds sink, threatening to slay it should it fail. The beast transformed into a deer and tried unsuccessfully to sink them, whereby the man slew the monster. The record goes on to say: "...He further sought out the water-dragon's fellows. Now the tribe of all the water-dragons filled a cave in the bottom of the pool. He slew them every one and the water of the river became changed to blood. Therefore that water was called the pool of Agatamori".{{r|Nihon67}}<ref>Tr. {{harvp|Aston|1896|loc='''1''', p. 299}}.</ref>
A river-god reported seen in Nintoku 11 (putatively 323 AD) is also regarded by commentators to be a mizuchi, due to paralleling circumstances. On that year, the {{illm|Mamuta dikes|ja|茨田堤}} built along {{ill|Yodo River|en|Yodo River|qid=Q1140505|lt=Yodo River|1=Yodo River}} kept getting breached and the Emperor guided by an oracular dream ordered two men, Kowa-kubi from {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|qid=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province|1=Musashi Province}} and Koromo-no-ko from {{ill|Kawachi Province|en|Kawachi Province|qid=Q1047150|lt=Kawachi Province|1=Kawachi Province}} be sought ought and sacrificed to the "'''River God'''" or {{Nihongo|[[:en:Kawa-no-kami|Kawa-no-kami]]|河伯|}}.{{Efn|Note that 河伯 in China designates the ''{{ill|Hebo|en|Hebo|qid=Q10521939|lt=Hebo|1=Hebo}}'' deity.}} One of the men, who resisted being sacrificed, employed the floating calabash and dared the River God to sink it as proof to show it was truly divine will that demanded him as sacrifice. A whirlwind came and tried, but the calabash just floated away, and thus he extricated himself from death using his wits. Although River God is not called ''mizuchi'' in the source, [[William George Aston|Aston]] has regarded the River God (Kawa-no-kami) and the ''mizuchi'' as equivalent.{{r|Aston1905_1_1501}}
{{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser{{!}}Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}} concludes, "From this passage, we learn that in ancient times human sacrifices were made to the dragon-shaped river-gods".{{r|Visser1913_139}} {{ill|Michael Foster (folklorist)|en|Michael Foster (folklorist)|qid=Q6830379|lt=Michael Dylan Foster|1=Michael Foster (folklorist)}} suggests this is "perhaps the first documented appearance of the water spirit that would become known popularly in Japan as the {{ill|Kappa (folklore)|en|Kappa (folklore)|qid=Q335140|lt=kappa|1=Kappa (folklore)}}".{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=2}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In [[Japanese folklore]] the ''kappa'' is a [[:en:water sprite|water sprite]] often considered benignly mischievous,{{sfnp|Foster|1998|pp=1, 4}} (and thus may appear unlike a sacrifice-demanding serpent). But the ''kappa'' can also be seen as sinister, reaching in and extracting the liver or the ''shirikodama'' from humans.{{sfnp|Foster|1998|p=6}}}}
A mizuchi is also mentioned in the {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|qid=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}, the ancient collection of Japanese poems. The {{ill|Waka (poetry)|en|Waka (poetry)|qid=Q737148|lt=tanka|1=Waka (poetry)}} poem #3833 composed by {{illm|Prince Sakaibe|ja|境部王}}<ref name=sakaibe-origtext>[[#manyoshu3833|''Man'yōshū'' #3833]] by Prince Saikabe, original text:"虎尓乗 古屋乎越而 青淵尓 鮫龍取将来 劒刀毛我"</ref> can be loosely paraphrased to mean "I could ride a tiger to leap over the Old Shack, to the green pool, to take down the ''mizuchi'' dragon there, if only I had a sword capable of doing just that".{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The shark (鮫) character in the poem's original text is emended to the mizuchi (蛟) character. {{illm|Kariya Ekisai|ja|狩谷棭斎}} in his annotation to the ''[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]'' remarks: "Considering the ''Manyōshū'' (quote follows).. the ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` shark-dragon´ is actually ''kōryō/jiaolong'' ` flood dragon´, and correctly read as ` ''midzuchi''´ 万葉集を按ずに.. 鮫龍即蛟龍也、宜しく美都知と訓ず".{{r|kariya1883}}}}{{r|Takeda1972_1PLUS|Ito2005_475PLUS}}
== Folklorist studies == Polymath {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|qid=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}}, in his essay {{Nihongo|''Jūnishi kō: mi(hebi)''|『十二支考』|"A Study of Twelve Animals of Chinese Zodiac"}} states "Even in our country (Japan), the various snakes that dwelled by water and were feared by people seemed to have been called ''mizuchi,'' or 'master of the water'".{{r|Minakata1917}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}} Here Minakata draws on [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] scholar {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}}' suggestion that the ''-chi'' signified an {{ill|Honorific|en|Honorific|qid=Q1326966|lt=Honorific|1=Honorific}}.{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Minakata misquoted Norinaga, but Norinaga said ''chi'' was the honorific. Minakata wrote: "When Motoori Norinaga said ''tsuchi'' was an honorific, he must have interpreted it as a master of water or somesuch 本居宣長はツチは尊称だと言ったは、水の主ぬしくらいに解いたのだろ".{{r|Minakata1916}}{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=116}} What Norinaga actually stated was "there are many examples of [deities' names that are called] so-and-so ''-zuchi'', where ''zu'' is a word akin to "of" while ''chi'' is an honorific 某豆知（なにづち）と云例あまたありて..豆（づ）は之（の）に通ふ辞、知（ち）は称名（たたへな）なり".{{r|Motoori1822}}}} As stated above folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita|Yanagita]] emphasized the meaning of ''chi'' as "spirit".{{r|yanagita_chiChar}}
=== Corruption into kappa === Minakata also conjectured that in some parts of the country, ''mizuchi'' eventually came to be regarded as creatures of the ''kappa'' kind. This is because the ''kappa'' creatures are known locally by many names that sound much like ''mizuchi'', such as ''mizushi'' (former {{ill|Noto Province|en|Noto Province|qid=Q1047671|lt=Noto Province|1=Noto Province}}, {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|en|Ishikawa Prefecture|qid=Q131281|lt=Ishikawa Prefecture|1=Ishikawa Prefecture}}), ''medochi'' ([[:en:Nanbu Domain|Nanbu]] region, parts of {{ill|Iwate Prefecture|en|Iwate Prefecture|qid=Q48326|lt=Iwate|1=Iwate Prefecture}}, {{ill|Aomori Prefecture|en|Aomori Prefecture|qid=Q71699|lt=Aomori|1=Aomori Prefecture}}, {{ill|Akita Prefecture|en|Akita Prefecture|qid=Q81863|lt=Akita|1=Akita Prefecture}}), ''mintsuchi'' ({{ill|Ezo|en|Ezo|qid=Q1040184|lt=Ezo|1=Ezo}}, now [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]]).{{sfnmp|Minakata|1984|1p=117|Minakata|1984b|2p=159}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Cf. other local synonyms of ''kappa'' such as ''medochi'' ([[:en:Ehime prefecture|Ehime prefecture]]) and ''mizushi'' ([[:en:Fukui prefecture|Fukui prefecture]]) mentioned by Asakawa Zen'an's ''Zen'an zuihitsu''.{{r|Asakawa1927_33940}}}}
Furthermore, in the lore of {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|qid=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} ({{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|qid=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture|1=Niigata Prefecture}}), the kappa was said to abhor the calabash gourd,<ref>Yanagita, Kunio (1914), ''Santō mintan shū'', p. 84, cited by Minakata</ref> which is reminiscent of the episodes in ''Nihon Shoki'' where the River God or ''mizuchi'' are challenged to submerge the calabashes.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984|p=117}} Similar observations are made by folklorists Yanagita{{r|Yanagita2014_133}} and Jun'ichirō Ishikawa.{{r|Ishikawa1985_4550645248}}
Minakata was also encouraged by the fact that the snake and the kappa (alongside the [[:en:suppon|suppon]] soft-shelled turtle) were grouped as three creatures known to kill humans in water by {{illm|Asakawa Zen'an|ja|朝川善庵}}'s essay ''Zen'an zuihitsu'' and conjectured that there used to be lore where sacred snakes which were "masters of the body of water" would transform into human form and wreak havoc, but terms such as ''mizushi'' became reserved for the kappa-kind, whereas the terms to refer to the "masters of the body of water" as ''mizuchi'' became forgotten.{{sfnp|Minakata|1984b|p=159}}

''mizuchi'') appears as adversary. * ''{{ill|Omamori Himari|en|Omamori Himari|qid=Q1203079|lt=Omamori Himari|1=Omamori Himari}}'' (manga, novella, anime) – the character Shizuku is a mizuchi. * ''[[:en:Our Home's Fox Deity.|Our Home's Fox Deity.]]'' – A [[miko]] priestess is possessed by a mizuchi. * ''{{ill|Samurai Deeper Kyo|en|Samurai Deeper Kyo|qid=Q621603|lt=Samurai Deeper Kyo|1=Samurai Deeper Kyo}}'' (manga) – {{ill|Demon Eyes Kyo|en|Demon Eyes Kyo|qid=Q3200962|lt=Demon Eyes Kyo|1=Demon Eyes Kyo}} uses an attack called "''mizuchi''" in his sword fighting style.
